name: Peroxycarboxylic (PAP) whitening
lead: PAP whitening uses phthalimidoperoxycaproic acid, a peroxycarboxylic acid marketed as a non-peroxide-based tooth whitening agent. It is promoted as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide products, which are associated with tooth sensitivity.[2]
Published evidence is sparse. A 2025 small study evaluated PAP activated by an 810-nm diode laser in fifteen patients with mild to moderate stains.[1] This article is correspondingly short.
infobox: Whitening toothpastes, strips and in-office gels

paras: A 2025 study in the Journal of Pharmacy & Bioallied Sciences enrolled fifteen patients with shades A2 to A3.5 and mild to moderate stains. After cleaning and polishing, a PAP agent was applied to the front surfaces of upper front teeth and activated with a diode laser, with assessments at baseline, immediately after treatment and at later follow-ups.[1] The abstract available does not give the quantitative results here.
No randomised trial comparing PAP with peroxide whitening was found.
Established whitening options are peroxide-based, with sensitivity and gum irritation the commonly reported side effects and peroxide strength regulated differently in the EU and US.[2]

refs.title: An Evaluation of the Efficacy of a Novel Non-Peroxide, Phthalimidoperoxycaproic Acid Teeth Whitening Agent in Conjunction with 810-nm Diode Laser

card.summary: Peroxide-free whitening agent (PAP) with one small laser-activated study behind it.
card.note: Published human evidence is a single 15-patient study.

quick.overview:
PAP is a non-peroxide whitening agent sold in some whitening products as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide.

Only a small 2025 study of fifteen patients with laser activation was found, so the evidence is thin.
quick.mechanism: A peroxycarboxylic acid is applied to teeth to oxidise stain compounds, optionally activated by light or laser.
quick.risks: Safety and sensitivity data are limited to that small study; no long-term data were found.
